short: A bishop hemmed in by its own pawns, sitting on the same colour squares.
body: A bishop only ever sees one colour. If your own pawns are fixed on that colour, the bishop spends the game looking at a wall it built itself, and in a closed position it can be worth less than a pawn.

The rule that follows is short enough to remember: put your pawns on the opposite colour to your bishop. When you cannot, get the bishop traded — a bad bishop is the piece you most want to swap, even for a knight.
It cuts the other way too. If your opponent has a bad bishop, decline exchanges that would relieve them, and play on the colour their bishop cannot defend.

diagram.caption: Black's light-squared bishop, behind its own light-square pawns on d5 and e6.
